origin_region: Pan-India · chai stalls and home kitchens
processing: A preparation rather than a leaf type: strong CTC black tea (usually Assam or an Assam, Dooars and South Indian blend) simmered with milk, sugar and spices such as green cardamom, ginger, cinnamon, cloves and black pepper, in endless local variations.
harvest_season: Not seasonal; made from year-round CTC production.
appearance_dry: Dark CTC granules, either plain or mixed with crushed cardamom pods, dried ginger, cinnamon bark and cloves.
appearance_liquor: Opaque tan to caramel-brown once the milk is in.
appearance_wet: Spent dark granules and spice fragments.
taste_profile: Sweet, creamy and warming: cardamom and ginger up front, a malty tea backbone and a peppery, clove-spiced finish.

brewing.notes: Simmer the tea and crushed spices in about 150 ml water for 3–4 minutes, add roughly 100 ml milk and sugar to taste, bring back to the boil once or twice, strain. Steeping tea bags in hot milk gives a thin, flat cup.

vintage_note: No vintage: masala chai is made from year-round CTC tea and sold as ready-mixed spiced loose tea or tea bags, as a spice blend to add to your own tea, and as sweetened chai concentrates and powders. Pre-mixed packs lose their spice aroma within months, so buy small and check the pack date; fresh CTC and whole spices crushed at the stove taste far better.
description:
Masala chai is India's everyday spiced tea: strong black tea boiled with milk, sugar and spices until the kitchen smells of cardamom. It is not a type of tea leaf but a way of making tea, and it is how most of India's enormous tea crop is actually drunk, at home and at the roadside stalls of the chai wallahs.

The tea underneath is almost always CTC, the granular black tea that India makes in huge volume, because only something that strong will cut through milk and sugar. The spice mix (the 'masala') changes from house to house: green cardamom and fresh ginger are nearly universal, cinnamon, cloves and black pepper are common, and fennel, star anise or nutmeg turn up regionally. Tea drinking on this scale is a twentieth-century habit in India, pushed hard by the tea industry in the early twentieth century, and the spices came from the vendors who adapted it to local taste.

The method matters more than the recipe. Simmer the spices and tea in water for a few minutes, add milk (roughly equal parts, or more milk for a richer cup), sweeten, bring it back to the boil once or twice and strain into small cups. Steeping tea bags in hot milk gives a thin, flat drink; so does using a delicate orthodox leaf. Mumbai 'cutting chai' is a half-glass of the same thing, extra strong.

In shops it comes as pre-mixed spiced loose tea or tea bags, as a spice blend to add to your own CTC, and as sweet 'chai latte' concentrates and powders that are mostly sugar; the Western chai latte is a cousin at best. Pre-mixed packs lose their aroma within months, so buy small, check the pack date and prefer whole spices.

For the best result at home, buy a good Assam CTC (BOP or PF grade) and whole green cardamom, and crush the pods just before they go in the pan.
